VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01344

All this is far removed from the image of gnosis held by its present-day opponents, and much closer to its authentic, fundamental meaning. When the study of the texts has advanced far enough, a systematic examination of the affinities among the gnostic traditions of the “religions of the Book” will become essential (we have already alluded to this in Book I). These affinities will need to be studied until the outlines of lost continents come into view.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01345

For now, we cannot insist strongly enough on the importance of the summaries H.-C. Puech has already published of his lectures on “Esoteric Doctrines and Gnostic Themes in the Gospel According to Thomas.” From these unusually rich and concentrated summaries, several themes emerge whose counterparts or variations can readily be found in Islamic gnosis—and, in their essentials, in the present “Tale of the Exile.” Central to them all is the theme of the “Angel,” already approached here in connection with the psalm addressed to “Perfect Nature.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01346
Puech's detailed analyses allow us to identify the following sequence of themes.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01347

Consider the simple statement “I know myself” as it appears in gnostic writings. Its analysis leads to a fundamental distinction between the “I” that is the knowing subject and the “self” that is the object known or recognized. The first is the self I experience in everyday life, immediately, within the world I perceive through my senses: the self exposed to the demands of this world of appearances, which largely directs and determines it. The second is what I am beyond appearances and the contingent conditions of the world of coming-into-being (genesis). This is my real, authentic, essential self—substantial and enduring. Inward knowledge may indeed reveal it to me as if it were within me. Yet at the same time it is perceived not as a fantasy, but as something objectively real, “a being that exists and abides in itself.” It would, in fact, be better to speak of the Self than of the ego: this is our eternal archetype, “ourselves in our eternity.” Its reality is so objective that it is experienced as the “personal angel,” the “person of light,” the “personal Guide”; or it may be represented by a garment of heavenly origin, or by an image, an icon (eikôn), a Double or “heavenly Twin.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01348

We have repeatedly encountered here the saying: “Whoever knows himself [his ‘soul,’ nafsa-ho] knows his Lord,” together with its variations: “Whoever knows himself knows his Imam. Whoever knows his Imam knows his Lord.” The spiritual masters of Islam have meditated on this saying, turning it over and over in every possible way; we have given examples. The relationship between the reflexive nafs (oneself, one's soul) and the subject pronoun man (the one who knows) corresponds exactly to the relationship between the knowing “I” and the “self” that is known or recognized in Puech's analysis.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01349

The correspondence is so close that in Shiite gnosis the Imam can take the place of the Self and perform the function of the “personal angel” in ancient gnosis. In Sohrawardî, this Self is represented by “Perfect Nature,” or by the initiating Angel encountered in his tales. We have already noted that for Sohrawardî and the Ishrâqîyûn—the philosophers of Eastern wisdom—the vision of “Perfect Nature” is bound up with the mystical story of Hermes.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01350

Other Sufi masters, Najmoddîn Kobrâ for example, speak of the “Witness in Heaven,” the Guide or “invisible master.” The “person of light” (phôteinos anthrôpos) in the Gospel According to Thomas, and the “Light-Self” or “Living Self” of Manichaean texts, have their exact counterparts in Najmoddîn Kobrâ and Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî: shakhs min nûr, shakhs nûrânî. The Ismailis know of a “form of light” that joins itself to the initiate at the moment of initiation. The “Perfect Human Being” (Anthrôpos teleios) is the Insân al-Kâmil, and so forth.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01351

Self-knowledge leads to union—or rather reunion—between the apparent self (the “I” that knows) and the transcendent Self. It means becoming again “what I am, and have never ceased to be, within myself.” Yet it seems wrong to speak here of a fusion in which the two become indistinguishable. Moreover, their meeting requires more than an act of reflection: it requires a return. The heavenly Self retains its objective reality, like the mirror before me in which I come to know and recognize myself.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01352

Since the mirror reveals my true “face” to me, to break it would destroy the very union it makes possible. There would be no “face” left, no knowledge “face to face.” This is also what emerges in the gnosis of the Imams from the theme of the Imam as the Face of God turned toward humanity and the Face of humanity turned toward God. The theme of return is essentially the theme of the birds' journey in 'Attâr, of exile in Sohrawardî's tale, and more generally of the “four spiritual journeys” in Islamic gnosis.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01353

The theme of the mirror embraces the whole mystery of Sîmorgh: the eternal Sîmorgh persists, yet so do the sî-morgh, the thirty birds. The hoopoe herself may become a Sîmorgh, while the eternal Sîmorgh remains. In Sohrawardî's tales, the relationship between the Self of light and the lower self is expressed above all through the “two wings of the angel Gabriel”: one wing of light, and the other not exactly a wing of darkness but a wing darkened, tinged with the reddish glow of evening twilight. Every human being reflects the image of the Angel of humanity.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01354

To free the “left wing” from darkness is not to destroy it, but to make it a wing of light once more, itself reflecting the luminous right wing. The soul as image or icon of the Angel, and the Angel as icon of the soul, is a familiar theme of Valentinian gnosis. In Sohrawardî, Perfect Nature is at once the “father” and the “child” in the spiritual world. The original relationship established by Eastern theosophy between the first lover and the first Beloved could not be abolished without abolishing the fundamental law of being, and of every being. This, as we have seen, is the meaning that Ishrâqî gnosis gives to the Qur'anic verse: “We have created all things in pairs” (51:49).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01355

There is also the theme of the personal pleroma. For each spiritual seeker, his “angel”—the ideal reality corresponding to his transcendent Self—is his own pleroma, his particular fullness of being: the form of everything he is, which defines him as an individual in the complete realization of his own existence. Every such individual fullness belongs within the universal Pleroma, the fullness of the spiritual world. “To know the pleroma within oneself” and “to know oneself within the pleroma” are two ways of saying the same thing. The Angel is our pleroma: our being in its fullness.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01356

This idea of an individual pleroma also follows from the relationship between the gnostic and his Perfect Nature. Their relationship exists within the pleroma of the angel Gabriel, the Angel of humanity (rabb al-nû' al-insânî), while Perfect Nature is, in turn, the angel present to each individual. This resolves the hesitation that sometimes appears among commentators as to whether the figure in question is the Angel of humanity or Perfect Nature. More than this, the dialogue between Constantine, son of Luke (Qostâ ibn Lûqâ), and his disciple 'Amalaq the Greek (see above, III, 5) may serve as an illustration of this relationship; compare also the “Personal City” discussed below in §5.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01357

Closely linked to this is the theme of spiritual ancestry. Gnosis is knowledge that saves because it saves the person by revealing his origin. Knowing what one is and who one is cannot be separated from knowing where one comes from and through whom one exists. To know his lineage, his descent, his family is, for the gnostic, to know his true homeland: to know what he was and where he was, and to recognize the order of beings to which he belongs. In the Gospel According to Thomas, to know oneself is, by that very fact, to know that one is a “son of the living Father.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01358

We find all this, point for point, in Islamic gnosis. To take only “The Tale of the Western Exile,” the revelation of spiritual ancestry that drives the entire drama appears at the outset and returns solemnly at the end. The exile is the son of shaykh al-Hâdî ibn al-Khayr, the Yemeni.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01359

We shall see later that this name designates the Active Intelligence, the Holy Spirit, the Angel of humanity. At the close of the tale, the Angel himself reveals to the exile, his “son,” that they share a whole succession of “ancestors.” This ancestral line is none other than the hierarchy of Angels or Intelligences in Islamic Neoplatonism and Ismaili gnosis. Here, too, we encounter the Neoplatonic idea of series or “chains” of souls proceeding from one of the gods. Proclus, we know, considered himself to belong to the “chain” of Hermes. The brothers whose family the exile belongs to in Sohrawardî's tale are represented by the “fish” playing in the “Spring of Life,” after passing through an ordeal like his own.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01360

That ordeal tore them from their origin and must end with their return to it: their return “home.” Saying 49 of the Gospel According to Thomas declares: “You will find the Kingdom, for you came from it, and to it you will return.” This implies that whoever knows his beginning also knows his end, because “to discover the beginning and to discover the end are one,” since “where the beginning is, there the end will be” (Saying 18). Gnosis is precisely what reveals this identity of beginning and end, meeting at a single point.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01361

This is the very theme of Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile”: “It is I who am the subject of this story; I have undergone a catastrophe.” Fallen from the world of light, from the world above or the Beyond, the exile lies imprisoned at the bottom of a well in the western city of Qayrawân, bound in iron chains.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01362

The place to which he must return is the place from which he came. We have already quoted the command in the “Epistle of the High Towers” (Risâlat al-abraj): “When you are told, ‘Return,’ this implies that there is a place where you were present before. And woe to you if you take the place of return to mean Damascus, Baghdad, or some other homeland in this world!” This is, moreover, one of the central themes of Islamic gnosis, expressed through the “two arcs” of descent (nozûl) and ascent (so'ûd), the place of origin (mabda') and the place of return (ma'âd).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01363

The idea that the end is reached by returning to the beginning—as in the movement of the compass to which Sohrawardî referred in the preceding tale—also corresponds to the Shiite theosophical understanding of the cycle of prophecy as a cycle of descent and the cycle of the Imamate as a cycle of ascent (see Book I above). An understanding of history as a circle that closes upon itself, while offering access at every moment to a reality beyond history, necessarily belongs with the idea of preexistence. Preexistence guarantees salvation because it guarantees continuity of being on a plane higher than this world of exile and the fall.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01364

The theme of certainty: gnosis assures the spiritual seeker that he will be saved from his present situation, and indeed cannot fail to be saved, because in truth he is already saved, here and now and for ever, since his origin and his destination are one.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01365

This is exactly the twofold assurance of salvation that the Angel communicates, at the end of “The Tale of the Exile,” to the exile who has found his way back to him. He is saved now—so completely saved already that, until his final return, he will be able to revisit the mystical Sinai whenever he wishes, borne there by ecstatic contemplation of the heavenly symbols.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01366

The theme of preexistence stands in relation to the theme of the Angel or of self-knowledge rather as the “answer” stands in relation to the “subject” in a musical fugue. It, too, receives an answer in turn: a certainty. Saying 19 of the Gospel According to Thomas declares: “Blessed is the one who was before coming into being.” Its answer is found in the Gospel According to Philip: “For he who is, has been and will be.” These sayings from our gnostic Gospels deserve to be inscribed in letters of gold in the ideal “Book” shared by all the gnostic traditions of the “religions of the Book.” “Preexistence implies the perpetuity of existence, permanence in Being.” To exist before becoming, to have existed before entering the world, the flesh, and chronological time: this “grounds the certainty of being, of never having ceased to be and of never ceasing to be oneself, beyond time as well as before it.” It is the certainty, we would say, that one is oneself a history which breaks open history in the ordinary sense of that word, because it is a history beyond history.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01367

The idea of preexistence is explicit in Sohrawardî's mystical tales. It is affirmed at the beginning of “The Tale of the Crimson Archangel” and both at the beginning and at the end of “The Tale of the Exile.” Admittedly, Sohrawardî's major systematic treatises sometimes show a certain ambiguity on this point, much to the irritation of Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî. A particular passage near the end of the Physics of the “Book of Crossroads and Conversations” (Mashârï wa Motârahât) might leave us uncertain.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01368

But we should note that these are precisely the outward, or exoteric, treatises; the inward, or esoteric, treatises written in the form of symbolic comparisons leave us in no doubt. We should add that the theme of preexistence echoes throughout Islamic gnosis. As we have said, Shiite thinkers generally accept preexistence as something taught by the holy Imams themselves. It is assumed in the spiritual interpretation of the mysterious verse about the “Covenant,” the pact made before earthly existence, when the question was put: “Am I not your Lord?” (7:171). This question keeps the believer's horizon open far beyond the moment of birth into this world.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01369

More still: our mystical theosophers—Mollâ Sadrâ, Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î—understand this question to be repeated from world to world, at every level at which being reveals itself, in each of the forty thousand universes spoken of in certain sayings (hadîth) of the Imams. Of these universes, our own world, the world of Adam's descendants, is the last. By their response to that question, human beings existing before the realm of becoming have themselves determined the meaning of their passage through this changing world, and therefore also what their final return to their origin will be.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01370

That is why we may say that our temporal existence is only an episode “between two eternities”; or, more precisely, that it leads from eternity to eternity. In Arabic, we would say: between azal and abad. And the theme of this return is the theme of “the gnostic meeting the Angel.” Its many variations will stand out more clearly if we take them up later (§4), after translating “The Tale of the Western Exile,” in which Sohrawardî brings together the great themes of his theosophy.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01371

Even now, however, we should note the close kinship between Sohrawardî's “Tale of the Exile” and the “Song of the Pearl,” also known as the “Hymn of the Soul” in the Acts of Thomas. This text gives voice to a central theme of Iranian spirituality, particularly in the Ishrâqî school. The comparison could, of course, carry us very far. R. Merkelbach, for his part, has examined the “Song of the Pearl” theme by theme, comparing it with Chariklea, the romance of Heliodorus (see above, Chapter V, 4), and identifying two parallel passages in Synesius and the emperor Julian.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01372

If the “Song of the Pearl” is to be regarded as a gnostic hymn, “The Tale of the Exile” presents itself in much the same way. Both deserve a place in the collection that may one day bring together all the scattered members—disjecta membra—of the vast family of gnosis. “The Tale of the Exile” could scarcely have been written differently had Sohrawardî himself first read the story of the young Iranian prince whom his parents send from the East to Egypt to recover the Pearl beyond price.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01373

Other echoes of the Pearl motif are found in Shiite gnosis. We may think of the tradition (hadîth) traced back to the Imam Ja'far, according to which the “Black Stone” set into a corner of the Ka'ba was once the “White Pearl” in Paradise: Adam's “angel,” subsequently sent to this earth to help Adam himself. The Imam's entire account has the form and significance of an initiation story, leading the initiate toward the “spiritual Temple.” We have studied it elsewhere.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01374

For the present, let us simply recall the story told in the “Song of the Pearl.” A young prince is sent by his parents, sovereigns of the “East,” his homeland, to Egypt to bring back the one precious Pearl. He removes the garment of light his parents had lovingly woven for him. He reaches the land of exile; he is the Stranger. He tries to pass unnoticed, but is recognized. He is given food that darkens his memory of his origin, until he forgets that he is a “king's son.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01375

Then one day a message arrives, borne by an eagle and signed by his father, his mother, and all the nobles of Parthia—that is, all the princes of the heavenly Pleroma. This distinctly Iranian way of locating them in the “East” agrees perfectly with the meaning Sohrawardî gives to “East” throughout his Eastern theosophy. The prince remembers who he is and the Pearl he was sent to recover. Then comes the “departure from Egypt,” the exodus, the great return to the East.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01376

As in gnosis generally, and as in Sohrawardî, the West (maghrib) represents the world of genesis, of earthly coming-into-being. Here that West is Egypt; for Sohrawardî it is the city of Qayrawân. (The prophet Mânî, too, in dying, departs from Egypt, Misraim.) The journey eastward ends when the prince puts on again the garment of light he had to set aside as a child. As we shall recall later (§4), this is one variation of the theme of “the gnostic meeting the Angel.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01377

The course of “The Tale of the Western Exile” runs parallel to that of the “Song of the Pearl.” The necessity bound up with the child's future destiny requires that this child of the “East” be sent into exile, into a “West” symbolized by Qayrawân. (The city lies in the western part of the Maghreb; perhaps its name, associated here with caravan, evokes the life of the soul imprisoned in this world as one long pilgrimage.) It is the city “whose inhabitants are oppressors.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01378

The young prince is chained and thrown to the bottom of a well. By night he awakens to the other world, but by day he falls back into the depths of the well. Will he remain there? Will he forget everything? Then one night a message comes from his family in the Beyond, brought by a hoopoe. The family wonders why he has not yet set out and urges him to leave without delay.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01379

Thus begins the journey home toward an East that cannot be found on our maps. The traveller climbs Mount Qâf, which we already know as a mountain belonging at once to the cosmos and to the inner world of the soul. He ascends as far as the mystical Sinai, dwelling place of the being who appears here as the Angel of humanity, whom the Neoplatonists call the Nous patrikos, the paternal Intelligence. (See also the short spiritual romance discussed below in §5, under the theme of the “Personal City,” which reproduces, theme for theme, the mystical drama just described.) We should also recall Proclus' remarkable spiritual interpretation of the “story” of Phaethon.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01380

Like the ta'wîl, the spiritual interpretation practised by our mystics, Neoplatonic interpretation works at several levels of understanding. There is the so-called “historical” interpretation, which touches only the outward meaning, the zâhir; there is the “physical” interpretation, operating at the level of symbols; and there is the “philosophical” interpretation, which amounts to “spiritual realism.” For the story of Phaethon is the story of a soul, indeed of a whole class of souls. It is a true history, but its truth is not located at the level of external events, of the everyday empirical ego. It belongs, rather, to the level of that “Self” to which I return when “I” come to know myself.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01381

And it is precisely when “I” make this return that “I” become the teller of the mystical tale, the hikâyat, as our authors themselves have described it. I tell my own story. “It is I who am the subject of this tale,” the author declares at the end of “The Tale of the Exile.” This history is not ordinary history, with the “thread of events” being spun out as the “days go by.” It is the narrator's own sacred history, his hierohistory. Once again we meet the question that has returned page after page throughout our study: What is history in its true sense?
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01382

What is a history that is itself truth, and that as such breaks through history in the ordinary sense, since ordinary history can reach only the self of appearances—one appearance among others? This problem lies at the heart of every spiritual interpretation of the “religions of the Book.” And because their spiritual masters have lived this experience, we find within these religions a gnosis that unveils the meaning beyond history of true history. Here we find ourselves entirely in agreement with certain recent pages by Gilbert Durand, who responds with philosophical courage and lucidity to one of those questionnaires fashionable today whose very terms already betray an impending surrender.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01383

Since the hikâyat constitutes the threefold unity described above, it is fundamentally wrong to treat hierohistory, “Sacred History,” as though it were merely a “historical and bygone” preface to ordinary history. Gilbert Durand writes: “The term and notion of Sacred History mean, above all, narrative, not an undertaking in archaeological reconstruction [...] For the liturgy consists in the reading, practice, exegesis, and interpretation of the sacred Narrative. It is an anti-history, just as the work of art, according to Malraux, is an ‘anti-destiny’: anti-history because it calls precisely for the repeated ‘recitation’ and ‘enactment’ of the narrative, recovering its ‘meaning’ for every instant, every cycle of time, every soul, and every moment of that soul. It does so against the ‘thread’ of History, against the positivist determinism of historical facts and blind events that carry human beings and empires through ascent, power, decline, and death.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01384

In these words we seem to hear, expressed perfectly in the philosophical language of our time, the principle of spiritual interpretation that we have already heard from the Fifth Imam and from Sohrawardî. The power of this history that breaks through history is preserved enduringly in the “phenomenon of the sacred Book,” the source of every spiritual tradition among the “religions of the Book,” whether Bible or Qur'an.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01385

Durand goes on: “Since the book is an originative narrative rather than a descriptive history claiming objectivity, we must reject the historical and archaeological thread in favour of an eschatological meaning”—a meaning concerned with our ultimate destiny. Whoever recites the “Book” in this way brings forth, in that very act, his own Book. Through Sohrawardî's spiritual interpretation, it is the Qur'anic verses themselves that will form the fabric of his “Tale of the Exile,” turning it into a liturgical recital.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01386

“Recite the Qur'an,” he said, “as though it had been revealed for you alone.” The orientation of this tale, and of all his tales, toward our ultimate destiny comes from putting this principle of interpretation into practice. This is what it means to understand “sacred history”: to acknowledge the reality of the imaginal world, the world of real spiritual images, and to lead the truth of appearances back toward that world, against the passage of time and against death.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01387

By contrast, those who now speak of “bringing the lives of the Saints into agreement with historical truth” have probably lost even the sense of this return. It is nothing other than the recurring act of liturgy, without which no spiritual tradition could continue to live the “Book.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic

2. Analysis of the Tale
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01388
In this tale, which we can now read in its original Arabic and in a Persian paraphrase , I propose to distinguish a prelude and three main acts, followed by a postlude or epilogue.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01389

Prelude. A short introduction gives Suhrawardi, the Shaykh of Illumination, an opportunity to define his own position in relation to Avicenna. Earlier, we saw how he distinguished his own “Eastern” philosophy from the philosophy Avicenna had conceived under the same name (above, Chapter I, § 2). Now he makes a further distinction, this time concerning the mystical tale itself. Suhrawardi refers to two works from Avicenna’s trilogy of visionary tales: the Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan and the Tale of Salaman and Absal.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01390
I have discussed Avicenna’s tales at length elsewhere and shall not return to them here .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01391

Let us simply note that Suhrawardi’s reference confirms that Avicenna did indeed compose a Tale of Salaman and Absal. Unfortunately, all that survives of it is the summary given by Nasir al-Din Tusi in his commentary on Avicenna’s Isharat. Twenty years earlier, Tusi had commented on the Hermetic version of the same story, which the great poet Jami (d. 898/1492) would later develop into an expansive poem, one of the masterpieces of Persian mystical epic. Elsewhere , I have compared the Hermetic and Avicennian versions of the Tale of Salaman and Absal. Suhrawardi expressly declares that this tale contains the mystical secret “entrusted to the symbols of the Sages.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01392

Yet, for all his praise of the Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan, he says that it fails to shed light on the mystical stage he has in mind. He stresses the significance of that stage for the soul’s ultimate destiny by naming it in Qur’anic terms—the “Great Upheaval” or “Great Overturning” . This is hardly surprising.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01393

The Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan does no more than introduce the disciple to the “East” and show him the road that leads there. The disciple must decide for himself whether to take that road, just as at the end of the Tale of the Crimson Archangel. Avicenna does take it in the Tale of the Bird.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01394

Nevertheless, the last lines of the Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan contain an unmistakable allusion. As Suhrawardi quotes them, they are indeed the lines we find at the close of Avicenna’s text: “It happens that some Solitaries among humankind migrate toward Him …” Those lines become the point of departure for Suhrawardi’s own tale. The Shaykh of Illumination thus fully recognized an intention in Avicenna that others have disputed. That recognition left him all the freer to tell his own story, which he called the Tale of the Western Exile.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01395

I. The first part of the tale (the passages I have numbered 1–14) might be called “The Fall into Captivity and the Escape.” It begins the story of the gnostic—the seeker of spiritual knowledge—in this world. That story, an episode “between two eternities,” begins with exile from the world of light, which is the East, and imprisonment in the world of material physis, or physical nature, which is the West. The protagonist, who also recites the story, sets out with his brother ’Âsim.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01396

The name means “one who protects, preserves, keeps safe,” but it can also mean, in a passive sense, “the protected one,” or “the one kept safe.” We naturally think that this brother must be the “heavenly Double,” the “self of light,” the Perfect Nature, the personal Angel. He would then correspond to the brother of the young Parthian prince in the Hymn of the Pearl, found in the Acts of Thomas .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01397

But in that story the mysterious brother remains in the Kingdom while the prince is sent into the darkness of Egypt to recover the Pearl. We saw earlier (Chapter V, § 4) that whenever a human soul descends, a Simorgh descends alongside it. Here, however, we encounter two striking differences.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01398
First, this “invisible” brother is himself held captive by the people of Qayrawân.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01399
Second, he does not reappear until passage 12, where the message received from the world beyond mentions him and calls on him, too, to free himself and set out on the road.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01400

The Persian commentator asks us to see in the brother “the contemplative faculty,” which belongs to the soul without involving the body. ’Âsim, he explains, is protected against every harmful or destructive force. Perhaps so.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01401

But this is precisely the kind of commentary against which I warned earlier (Chapter IV, § 4). I would suggest another approach. To interpret a mystical tale is not to drag it back down to the familiar certainties of philosophical logic, as though explaining a symbol meant that the thing expressing it could simply disappear. This is the greatest deception in the modern enterprise of “demythologizing.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01402

Consider what actually happens: the hero and his brother travel from “the region beyond the river” into the Western land to hunt birds along the shores of the Green Sea. We could translate this into philosophical language: they descend from the higher world into the world of darkness so that, through knowledge, they may transform what is perceived by the senses into what can be grasped by the intellect, and thereby attain the perfection of a soul raised to the state of Nous, or Intellect. Certainly.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01403

But if we hear only that explanation and put it in place of the tale, we lose the meaning of the metaphysical epic. Gnosis is gone; hikâyat, the living act of mystical storytelling, is gone. All that remains is a lesson in philosophy.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01404

The two brothers reach the most distant city of this “West,” marking the soul’s farthest evening decline—the very opposite of Ishrâq, the illumination of dawn (illuminatio matutina). That city is Qayrawân, which plays the same symbolic part here that Egypt plays in the Hymn of the Pearl. Its inhabitants seize the brothers and bind them when they discover that the newcomers are children of the world of Light, sons of the shaykh al-Hâdî ibn al-Khayr, the Yemeni.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01405

Since they are his “children,” it is indeed their “father” whom the exile will rejoin at the end of the tale, on the mystical Sinai at the summit of Mount Qâf. We therefore have three linked designations for the same Intellect: the Angel of humanity, the Holy Spirit, who is for human beings the Nous patrikos or paternal Intellect, and the Active Intellect of the Avicennian philosophers, the tenth being in the archangelic hierarchy .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01406
The name al-Hâdî means “the Guide.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01407

Let us retain that word: we shall return to it in § 4, comparing its meaning in other settings that illuminate the tale’s concern with our ultimate destiny. Ibn al-Khayr literally means “son of the Good.” The Neoplatonic allusion is plain. Muslim philosophers knew a work by Proclus on the “Pure Good” . At the end of the story we shall hear of the “Supreme Ancestor,” Light of Light, the one to whom all the angelic hierarchies ultimately lead, and who, like Melchizedek, has neither father nor grandfather.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01408

Al-Hâdî proceeds from this Pure Good, the source from which being comes into manifestation: he is its “son.” Why, then, is he called “the Yemeni”? Because southern Arabia, Yemen, and the land of Sheba occupy an important place in the visionary geography of these mystical writers. Yemen is associated with the “right-hand side” of the valley, where the divine voice called to Moses from the Burning Bush (Qur’an 28:30). Many hadiths, or traditions of the Prophet, could be cited to illustrate this meaning.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01409

Mir Damad, the great theologian of the school of Isfahan, was particularly fond of quoting this one: “Faith comes from Yemen; divine wisdom is Yemeni” . Yemen is thus equivalent to “East” in the Illuminationist sense. “Yemeni philosophy” stands in the same contrast to Peripatetic philosophy as “Eastern philosophy” does. Here the visionary experience even agrees with ordinary geography, since Yemen really does lie east of Qayrawân. It is worth noting, too, that the biographer of Christian Rosenkreutz, whose name gave rise to that of the Rosicrucians, sent his hero on his “quest for Knowledge” as far as the sages of Yemen .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01410

High above the deep well into which the prisoners have been thrown stands a fortified castle with many towers. It is the castle formed by the celestial Spheres, crowned by the heaven of the Fixed Stars, where the constellations of the zodiac are carried—the abrâj, plural of borj, meaning castles or high towers. The prisoners are allowed to climb to this castle and attempt a spiritual ascent through the Spheres, but only at night.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01411

Here we meet again the symbolism of night whose ambiguity I discussed earlier (Chapter IV, § 4). It appeared in the Tale of the Crimson Archangel. In that story, the child Zal is with Simorgh during the day—that is, he is present in the world of light—while at night he is entrusted to the care of the anima sensitiva, the soul’s sensory life.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01412

In The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings (above, p. 220), the prologue shows the Child, the heavenly human being, casting off his bonds as soon as night falls. These are the bonds that fetter the children of Earth: the constraints of sensory perception that keep earthly people imprisoned, asleep in their soul’s unawareness. It is, then, night for the senses: active Imagination and imaginative perception have complete freedom.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01413

Yet this night of the senses is itself the dawning of the mystical day, the Ishrâq. The visionary opens the door of the khângâh, the Sufi lodge. In other words, at the threshold of awareness beyond ordinary consciousness, he opens the secret door onto the unexplored desert. It is the entrance to the world beyond the senses, the world of Mystery (ghayb), and the beginning of the road to the spiritual and angelic world.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01414

When day breaks again, however—when the world of “normal” knowledge returns—the door leading outside, into the free expanse of the spiritual world, is closed, and the door onto the city is opened . That city is Qayrawân, where people go about their business while captives dwell among them, able to escape only under cover of the “night.” This is everything that passages 6–9 of the Tale of the Western Exile are meant to tell us .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01415

Within this symbolism, then, day can appear as night and night as day, depending on whether we look from the “Eastern” or “Western” side . The same double meaning lies at the heart of esoteric interpretation in Sufism, Ismailism, and Shiism alike. The hidden meaning (bâtin) is both the night of what lies concealed and the daylight of spiritual truth. The outward meaning (zâhir) is both the daylight of the religious Law’s literal wording and the darkness that enslaves bodies, minds, and souls.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01416

And so the exile and his brother “climb up during the night and descend during the day” (passage 9). Day is the bottom of the well, where “darkness piles upon darkness.” Night is the sight of lightning over Yemen, the forbidden region, the Angel’s “East.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01417

It is from that forbidden region that the message arrives, on one particular night. A hoopoe brings it on a night of the full moon. The commentator sees the hoopoe as “inspiration of the heart” and the full-moon night as “cleansing away the stains and impurities given off by material nature.” I have no objection, provided we do not stop there.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01418

Recall that the full-moon night was already announced as a motif in the preceding tale; it will appear again later in this one. As for the hoopoe, recall the passage in which we saw it take flight in spring and become a Simorgh (above, Chapter V, § 3). Here, in the Tale of the Western Exile, the liturgical recitation is already under way.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01419

To identify itself and deliver its message, the hoopoe “recites” the Qur’anic verses in which the hoopoe from the land of Sheba—that is, from the direction of Yemen—presents itself to Solomon and tells him of Bilqis, the Queen of Sheba. The message also recalls the letter sent to the young Parthian prince in the Hymn of the Pearl.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01420

Other echoes can be heard. “Hold fast to our cord,” the message commands. This is precisely what Hermes heard from his “father” when he called for help amid the dangers of his ecstatic vision (below, § 4, II). There, the cord was a “ray of light,” an illumination from the sacred world. Here it means something similar, but the image is written in a cipher that is difficult to read: “the Dragon of the heaven of the Moon in the spiritual world, which rules over the shores of the eclipse.” I believe the cipher can be deciphered as follows.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01421

Astronomy speaks of the Dragon’s head and tail—Tannîn in Arabic, Jawzahar in Persian—as the “nodes of the Moon,” the points where the Moon’s orbit crosses the Sun’s apparent path, making eclipses possible. The ascending node, where the Moon begins to move north of the ecliptic, is the “Dragon’s head” (ra’s al-Tannîn), the northern node. The descending node, where it begins to move south of the ecliptic, is the “Dragon’s tail” (dhanab al-Tannîn), the southern node .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01422

But our subject is not astronomy. The Dragon is associated with an eclipse, while everything takes place “in the heaven of the Moon in the spiritual world.” And the Moon in the spiritual heaven is none other than the mystic himself. What we learned earlier about the “Jewel-that-Illumines-the-Night” (above, Chapter V, § 3) enables us finally to read the cipher. When the Moon is closest to the Tûbâ Tree—that is, to the Sun—it appears to us to have become wholly shadow: we can no longer see it, just as we cannot see the Grail once freed from its covering of skin.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01423

Yet in relation to the Sun it is wholly light. That is what the return from Western exile means: an eclipse, a withdrawal from the sight of the inhabitants of the “city of oppressors,” occurring in the very measure that the mystic, disappearing from his own visible self, is completely filled with the light of the spiritual Sun. The imagery is coherent throughout. That is why the Dragon will be mentioned once more (passage 33), at a decisive moment of the Return.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01424

The last two passages of this first part of the tale complete the message received from the “East” and give directions for the stages of the journey. These are encoded in Qur’anic verses. In the “valley of the ants” (27:18), the pious anonymous commentator sees only an allusion to covetousness.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01425

But the first chapter of Suhrawardi’s Language of the Ants (Loghât-e mûrân) suggests something quite different. At dawn, ants emerge from the darkness of their hiding place and are astonished to see drops of dew on the plants. They argue endlessly over where the drops came from. As the sun grows warmer, however, the dew is drawn upward, for everything returns to its origin.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01426

The Qur’anic verses cited in that work echo those “recited” here. When you reach the valley of the ants, therefore, “shake out the hem of your robe”—that is, abandon futile arguments—and recite: “To Him is our resurrection” (67:15). The commands grow more urgent: let your people perish, and your wife too—in other words, everything bound up with the desires of the flesh.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01427

The Qur’anic verses here recall the fate of Lot’s wife, who could not be saved because she was among those who remained behind (29:31), while Sodom’s people were destroyed by a storm at sunrise (15:51–73). One must board Noah’s ark, which here, as in Shiite gnosis, is the mystical vessel of salvation. “In the name of God, let it sail and come to harbour” (11:43).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01428

II (passages 15–36). The pilgrims—the exile and his brother ’Âsim—set out, reach the far edge of the shadow, and there board Noah’s ark . At that moment, the narrator tells us, “the sun was directly above our heads.” This image becomes clear if we recall what Suhrawardi says elsewhere about the “quest for the East” and the “sacred experience” (above, Chapter II, § 2). Reaching the far edge of the shadow means reaching the boundary of the sublunar material world, the limit of the “West.”
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01429

Here the “middle East” begins: the imaginal world, the proper home of visionary stories and dreams. It is the realm in which actions such as these acquire their meaning—actions intended to free the soul from the physiological apparatus of the material body. Neither these actions nor their consequences are accessible to sensory perception. They run counter to the laws of the physical world: walking on water, reaching the heavens, the folding inward of time and space, and so forth.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01430

In short, this is entry into the world experienced by certain mystical travellers (sâlikûn) when, as the Shaykh of Illumination says elsewhere, the light surrounding them stands “at the zenith over certain cities of the middle East.” This is the “eighth clime,” between the West of the physical world and the East of the higher Malakût, the spiritual kingdom .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01431

Elsewhere we find further, converging indications of what the “hour of noon” means, when the sun stands at its highest point. At the end of his commentary on the “hadith of the White Cloud,” for instance, Qazi Sa’id Qummi explains that noon, the hour when the pilgrims’ extraordinary journey into the Malakût with the Imam comes to an end, signifies that they have now attained the spiritual maturity needed to enter that realm. They have reached the “equator” of human reality, the perfect balance of the walâyat—the spiritual authority and bond of devotion—belonging to the “Seal of the walâyat” .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01432

We might also recall a moment in the vision of the alchemist Zosimos. Behind the sword-bearer coming from the East, another figure appears, carrying a round object of dazzling beauty and whiteness, called “Position of the Sun at Midheaven” . This is exactly the allusion in the Tale of the Western Exile.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01433

Yet its narrator has told us that he and his brother escaped from prison “during the night.” We therefore have further confirmation that the meanings of day and night are reversed when we pass from the sensory to the suprasensory world. This reversal, the appearance of a “midnight sun,” prepares us for everything that follows .
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01434

What follows is a swift triumph of liturgical recitation of the Qur’an. In a handful of passages it achieves the conditions of perfect hikâyat, defined earlier as a threefold unity realized in the very act of recitation: the unity of the reciter, the deeds recited, and the hero whose deeds they are (above, Chapter IV, § 5, and Chapter VI, § 1).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01435

The narrator of the Tale of the Western Exile is not reconstructing the historical and archaeological meaning of the Qur’an. Suhrawardi is putting his own precept into practice: “Recite the Qur’an as though it had been revealed for your own case.” As a Neoplatonist, the Shaykh of Illumination is himself proof that there is no incompatibility between the Platonic vision of the world beyond, expressed through space, and the Qur’anic or biblical vision of the world beyond, expressed through the unfolding of human history in time.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01436

Indeed, it is precisely that other space which opens a place for this sacred history. It allows the events to remain forever ready to happen and to happen again. The result is not a chronicle but a liturgy—a liturgy in which time can be reversed within a space that time itself brings into being.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01437

Through the liturgical recitation of Qur’anic verses, the narrator relives the drama of the prophets. His journey toward the mystical Sinai carries him from one prophet of his own being to another, folding inward from one heaven of his being to the next, until he reaches the astrum in homine, the star within the human being.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01438

One after another, the narrator becomes Noah, Lot, Moses, Dhu’l-Qarnayn (Alexander), Solomon. He is Noah, separated from his son by the waters because the son was not truly of his family (passage 16). The commentator identifies this son with the vital spirit (rûh haywânî), while the nurse cast into the sea (passage 19) would be the physical spirit (rûh tabî’î).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01439

The narrator is Lot, who knows that his people, abandoned to wrongdoing, will be destroyed the next morning, at the hour of Ishrâq (passage 18). He is Moses travelling with the mysterious prophet Khezr (Khadir), who initiates him (passage 20). Noah’s ark sails so boldly that it crosses the gap separating the story of Moses from that of Alexander in sura 18. Now the pilgrim reaches Mount al-Jûdî, where Noah’s ark came to rest, and faces the peoples of Gog and Magog (Yâjûj and Mâjûj, passage 21).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01440

There he is Alexander, building a barrier to protect the human microcosm—the human being understood as a little universe—against the assaults of subhuman forces (passage 22). He can do so because he is also Solomon, at whose disposal are the spring of molten copper and the spirits who labour in his service. These allusions are obscure; they may have an alchemical meaning connected with the “resurrection body.” I would be reluctant to force an explanation on them.
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01441

Still, we should recall how often the image of a piece of iron heated until it glows recurs in different settings, the iron becoming a bearer of the fire’s properties. The image can suggest either the mystery of mystical union (unio mystica) or the mystery of the Imam’s being. There is another allusion to the cities of ’Âd and Thamûd, two peoples of ancient Arabia who rejected the summons of the prophets sent to them (passage 24).
VI. “The Tale of the Western Exile” and the Gnostic Epic
passage-en-01442

Then comes a series of actions whose literal description gives an impression of magnificent incoherence. The commentator labours—or rather strains—to draw up a meticulous inventory of correspondences that are at once commonplace and unconvincing. The old psychology distinguished so many faculties of the soul that one or another can always be made to fit a given image.
